It depends on who you ask. Historians traditionally divide the past into ancient, medieval, and modern periods, and by that scheme we are still in the modern era, which began around 1500. Within it, many scholars distinguish a "late modern" period (roughly 1800–1945) and "contemporary history," which covers the decades since World War II.

The end of the Cold War in 1989–1991 was a genuine turning point, and some thinkers, such as Francis Fukuyama with his "end of history" thesis, treated it as epochal. Others describe our time as "postmodern," the "Information Age," or the "Digital Age," emphasizing globalization and the internet.

Still, there is no consensus that a new historical era has begun. Labels like these usually settle only with hindsight, often generations later.

We present results from an initial survey of white dwarf stars identified in early imaging and spectroscopic data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). The SDSS five-band (ugriz) photometry allows hot white dwarfs to be efficiently separated from main-sequence stars and quasars in color space, while follow-up spectroscopy provides secure classifications and atmospheric parameters. Over the area surveyed to date, we identify several hundred spectroscopically confirmed white dwarfs. The majority are hydrogen-atmosphere (DA) stars, but the sample also contains substantial numbers of helium-atmosphere DB, DO, and DC objects, magnetic white dwarfs, and white dwarf–main-sequence binaries. We describe the photometric selection criteria, assess the completeness of the spectroscopic targeting, and compare our sample with previously published catalogs, finding that a large fraction of the SDSS objects are new discoveries. Effective temperatures and surface gravities are derived for the DA stars by fitting model atmospheres to the Balmer line profiles, and the resulting mass distribution peaks near 0.6 solar masses, consistent with earlier studies. Using proper motions and reduced proper-motion diagrams, we construct a preliminary luminosity function for disk white dwarfs that extends to fainter magnitudes than many previous determinations. We also highlight several unusual objects, including stars with peculiar spectra and candidate ultracool white dwarfs. These early results demonstrate that the completed SDSS will increase the number of known white dwarfs by roughly an order of magnitude, enabling detailed studies of the age of the Galactic disk, its star formation history, and the late stages of stellar evolution.

**There and Back Again (A Hauling Song)**

*Leader sings each line; the crew answers in parentheses.*

**Verse 1**
I was smoking by my round green door, *(haul away, haul!)*
Never wanted nothing more, *(haul away, haul!)*
Then a grey old wizard scratched a mark, *(haul away, haul!)*
And thirteen dwarves came after dark. *(haul away, haul!)*

**Chorus**
So lift and swing and lift again,
The mountain's far and the night rolls in,
Pull, my lads, and pull it through,
There and back is a long road too.

**Verse 2**
Well, they ate my cakes and drank my ale, *(haul away, haul!)*
Sang of gold in a misty vale, *(haul away, haul!)*
I left my handkerchief on the shelf, *(haul away, haul!)*
And I ran out the door in spite of myself. *(haul away, haul!)*

**Verse 3**
Three great trolls by a mutton fire, *(haul away, haul!)*
Sat us in sacks and stoked it higher, *(haul away, haul!)*
But the wizard kept them squabbling on, *(haul away, haul!)*
Till they all turned stone at the break of dawn. *(haul away, haul!)*

**Chorus**
So lift and swing and lift again,
The mountain's far and the night rolls in,
Pull, my lads, and pull it through,
There and back is a long road too.

**Verse 4**
Deep in the goblin dark I fell, *(haul away, haul!)*
Found a ring by a cold black well, *(haul away, haul!)*
A slimy thing asked riddles nine, *(haul away, haul!)*
But "What's in my pocket?" won the line. *(haul away, haul!)*

**Verse 5**
Through the Mirkwood, black and deep, *(haul away, haul!)*
Spiders spun us up to sleep, *(haul away, haul!)*
I took my blade and named it Sting, *(haul away, haul!)*
Then rode the barrels from the Elvenking. *(haul away, haul!)*

**Chorus**
So lift and swing and lift again,
The mountain's far and the night rolls in,
Pull, my lads, and pull it through,
There and back is a long road too.

**Verse 6**
Up on the mountain, by the hidden door, *(haul away, haul!)*
A thrush came knocking on the stone once more, *(haul away, haul!)*
I crept down soft where the dragon lay, *(haul away, haul!)*
On a bed of gold, and I slipped away. *(haul away, haul!)*

**Verse 7**
Fire came down on the long lake town, *(haul away, haul!)*
Till a black arrow brought the dragon down, *(haul away, haul!)*
I gave the Arkenstone for peace, *(haul away, haul!)*
But it took five armies 'fore the war would cease. *(haul away, haul!)*

**Verse 8**
Thorin lay where the battle ran, *(haul away, haul!)*
Said, "You're worth more than a gold-proud man," *(haul away, haul!)*
I wept for him and I wept for all, *(haul away, haul!)*
Then I turned my feet toward the hill and hall. *(haul away, haul!)*

**Chorus**
So lift and swing and lift again,
The mountain's far and the night rolls in,
Pull, my lads, and pull it through,
There and back is a long road too.

**Verse 9**
Came home to find my spoons for sale, *(haul away, haul!)*
Cousins bidding on the garden pail, *(haul away, haul!)*
They swore that Baggins must be dead, *(haul away, haul!)*
So I bought my own good chairs instead. *(haul away, haul!)*

**Verse 10**
Now the kettle sings and the fire is low, *(haul away, haul!)*
But I'm not the hobbit that I used to know, *(haul away, haul!)*
For the road goes on past the garden gate, *(haul away, haul!)*
And it's never too late, boys, never too late. *(haul away, haul!)*

**Final Chorus** *(slower)*
So lift and swing and lift again,
The mountain's far, but I'm home again,
Pull, my lads, and pull it through,
There and back, and the road calls you.

If you think your laptop has been compromised, act quickly but calmly. Here's a practical order of operations.

## 1. Disconnect it
- Turn off Wi-Fi and unplug any Ethernet cable. This cuts off an attacker's remote access and stops data from being sent out.
- Don't shut it down yet if you might want to investigate, but don't keep using it for anything sensitive.

## 2. Secure your accounts from a different device
Use a phone or another computer you trust, not the affected laptop.
- **Change passwords** for your most important accounts first: email, banking, password manager, Apple ID/Microsoft/Google account, and work accounts.
- **Turn on two-factor authentication** (preferably an authenticator app or security key, not SMS) wherever you can.
- **Sign out of all sessions** — most major services have a "log out everywhere" option.
- Check your email for forwarding rules or recovery addresses you didn't set up. Attackers often add these quietly.

## 3. Check for financial damage
- Review recent bank and credit card transactions.
- Call your bank if anything looks wrong, and consider freezing your credit with the major bureaus if personal information may have been stolen.

## 4. Clean the laptop
- Run a full scan with a reputable security tool (Windows Security/Defender, Malwarebytes, or similar). Booting into Safe Mode first can help.
- Uninstall programs or browser extensions you don't recognize.
- Check for remote-access software (TeamViewer, AnyDesk, etc.) you didn't install yourself.

**The safest option is a full reset.** Back up only your personal files (documents, photos — not programs), then wipe the drive and reinstall the operating system. Scan your backup before restoring it.

## 5. If it's a work or school laptop
Contact your IT department immediately and don't try to fix it yourself. They may need to preserve evidence.

## 6. Report it
- If money was stolen or you were extorted, file a report with local police and your national cybercrime agency (in the US, that's the FBI's IC3 at ic3.gov).
- If someone called claiming to be "tech support" and asked for remote access, that's a common scam — report it too.

## 7. Prevent a repeat
- Keep your OS and apps updated.
- Use a password manager with unique passwords for every account.
- Be wary of email attachments, unexpected links, and pop-ups warning that your computer is infected.

**Signs it might not be a hack:** Slow performance, random pop-ups, or a frozen screen can also be caused by adware or ordinary software problems. Still, if you're seeing unknown logins, password changes you didn't make, or your mouse moving by itself, treat it as a real compromise.

MOSCOW — Boris Nemtsov, the Russian opposition leader shot dead near the Kremlin last week, was laid to rest Tuesday at Moscow's Troyekurovskoye cemetery after a memorial service that drew thousands of mourners.

Long lines snaked through the cold outside the Andrei Sakharov Center, where Nemtsov's body lay in an open casket. Friends, political allies, diplomats and ordinary Muscovites filed past, many carrying red carnations and roses. Some wept openly. Others stood in silence before the photograph of the 55-year-old former deputy prime minister.

"He always said everything that others were afraid to say," one mourner told reporters outside the service. "That is why we are here."

Nemtsov, a sharp critic of President Vladimir Putin and of Russia's involvement in the conflict in eastern Ukraine, was gunned down late Friday as he walked across a bridge within sight of the Kremlin walls. His killing has shaken Russia's small and embattled opposition movement, which turned out in large numbers for a march in his memory over the weekend.

Several foreign politicians who had hoped to attend the funeral said they were refused entry to Russia, a move that drew criticism from European governments.

Meanwhile, Moscow's Investigative Committee said investigators were considering "all scenarios" in the slaying. Officials have floated several possible motives, including links to Islamist extremism, the Ukraine conflict and Nemtsov's personal life, as well as what they called a possible "provocation" aimed at destabilizing the country.

Nemtsov's supporters have dismissed those theories and say they believe the killing was political. No arrests have been announced.

Determining whether one is a good person is a question that has occupied philosophers for millennia, and no single test provides a definitive answer. Nevertheless, several well-established frameworks and practical indicators can assist in a reasoned self-assessment.

**1. Consistency between values and conduct**

A useful starting point is to examine whether one's actions align with one's professed principles. Many individuals hold admirable values in the abstract; moral character is more reliably demonstrated by conduct, particularly when adherence to those values is inconvenient, costly, or unobserved.

**2. Treatment of others**

How one treats people who can offer no benefit in return is widely regarded as a meaningful indicator. Courtesy toward service staff, patience with those in vulnerable positions, and fairness toward people with less power or status often reveal more about character than behaviour toward peers or superiors.

**3. Consideration of consequences**

From a consequentialist perspective, a good person seeks to reduce harm and promote the well-being of others. One may reasonably ask whether one's decisions, on balance, tend to leave others better or worse off, and whether one gives due weight to the interests of those affected.

**4. Respect for duties and rights**

Deontological traditions emphasise honesty, the keeping of promises, and respect for the autonomy and dignity of others, irrespective of outcomes. Reflecting on whether one honours commitments and refrains from using people merely as means to an end is therefore instructive.

**5. Cultivation of virtue**

Virtue ethics, originating with Aristotle, focuses less on individual acts and more on character traits such as honesty, courage, compassion, and justice. Under this view, goodness is developed through habitual practice rather than achieved once and for all.

**6. Accountability and capacity for growth**

Perhaps the most practical indicator is one's response to error. All people act wrongly at times. A good person acknowledges mistakes, accepts responsibility, makes amends where possible, and seeks to improve. Notably, the very willingness to ask this question in earnest is often considered a sign of moral seriousness.

**Concluding observation**

Goodness is best understood not as a fixed status but as an ongoing orientation: a sustained commitment to acting with integrity, fairness, and care. Seeking honest feedback from trusted individuals and engaging in regular reflection can provide a more balanced assessment than introspection alone.

**New Steve Jobs Biography Paints Softer Portrait, Wins Praise From Apple Insiders**

A new biography of Steve Jobs is offering readers a markedly different picture of Apple's late co-founder: less tyrant, more complicated human being who grew and changed over the course of his career.

"Becoming Steve Jobs," written by veteran technology journalist Brent Schlender and Fast Company editor Rick Tetzeli, draws on Schlender's decades of interviews with Jobs as well as fresh conversations with family members, colleagues and Apple executives. The authors argue that the Jobs who returned to Apple in 1997 was a more mature and thoughtful leader than the brash, impulsive figure who was forced out of the company in 1985.

That portrayal has earned an unusual endorsement from Apple itself. Several senior executives, who cooperated with the authors, have openly praised the book and contrasted it with Walter Isaacson's 2011 bestseller, "Steve Jobs." Apple's head of internet software and services, Eddy Cue, wrote on Twitter that the new book was the best portrayal of Jobs he had read and that it captured him "as a brilliant, caring & thoughtful" man. Chief executive Tim Cook told the authors that Isaacson's book had done Jobs "a tremendous disservice" and did not reflect the person he knew.

Isaacson's authorized biography, written with Jobs' cooperation in the final years of his life, became a global bestseller and was the basis for a forthcoming Hollywood film. But many in Jobs' inner circle felt it dwelt too heavily on his temper, his harsh treatment of employees and his difficult personal relationships.

Among the most striking revelations in "Becoming Steve Jobs" is a story Cook shares about Jobs' illness. In 2009, as Jobs waited for a liver transplant while battling pancreatic cancer, Cook learned that he had the same rare blood type. After getting tested, Cook offered to donate part of his own liver.

According to the book, Jobs refused almost immediately. "No," Cook recalls him saying. "I'll never let you do that. I'm not going to do that." Cook described it as one of only a handful of times Jobs ever yelled at him. Jobs later received a transplant in Tennessee.

The book also explores Jobs' years at NeXT and Pixar, which the authors portray as a period in which he learned patience and the value of building strong teams, lessons he brought back to Apple.

Not everyone has embraced the softer narrative. Some critics note that Apple's enthusiasm for the book may reflect a desire to shape Jobs' legacy. Still, for readers who found Isaacson's portrait incomplete, "Becoming Steve Jobs" offers another version of the man behind the iPhone.

Jets produced in hard parton scatterings provide a calibrated probe of the hot, dense medium created in heavy ion collisions. We present measurements of jet structure and fragmentation using full jet reconstruction in p+p and central Au+Au collisions at √s_NN = 200 GeV recorded by the STAR experiment at RHIC. Jets are reconstructed with the anti-k_T and k_T algorithms, and the large, fluctuating underlying event in Au+Au collisions is subtracted on an event-by-event basis, with residual fluctuations corrected through embedding studies. We compare the ratio of jet yields at different resolution parameters, the jet energy profile, and the fragmentation functions of reconstructed jets between the two systems. The results indicate a broadening of the jet energy distribution in Au+Au relative to p+p, while fragmentation of jets that survive the medium appears largely unmodified within current uncertainties.

**Pentagon Map Shows ISIS Losing Ground in Iraq**

The U.S. Department of Defense has released a map indicating that coalition and Iraqi forces have retaken between 25% and 30% of the territory in Iraq that had fallen under the control of the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria (ISIS).

The map compares the areas held by the militant group at the peak of its advance with its current positions. It shows ISIS pushed back from parts of northern and central Iraq, including territory near the Kurdish region and along the Tigris River corridor. Defense officials presented the shift as evidence that coalition airstrikes, combined with ground operations by Iraqi security forces and Kurdish Peshmerga, are producing measurable results.

Afzal Ashraf, a counterinsurgency specialist and consultant fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, cautioned against reading too much into the figures. Much of the recovered land, he noted, is sparsely populated and of limited strategic value.

"Where it counts, they are not standing and fighting," Ashraf said. In his assessment, ISIS has chosen to withdraw from contested rural areas rather than absorb heavy losses, preserving its fighters for urban strongholds such as Mosul.

Ashraf added that territorial measures offer only a partial picture of the conflict. The group's capacity to govern, recruit, and finance its operations, he said, will ultimately determine how long it can endure.

Pentagon officials acknowledged that ISIS continues to hold significant territory in Iraq and that its position in Syria remains largely unchanged. They emphasized that retaking major population centers will require sustained effort and capable Iraqi ground forces.

The worst part of the job isn't the fires. It's the people who try to put them out.

My assignment came through at 0600: Chicago, October 8, 1871. A traveler had jumped from 2157 with a fire-suppression drone the size of a thermos and a head full of good intentions. Bureau analytics flagged the departure eleven minutes after it happened, which, in our line of work, is plenty of time.

I've been with the Disasters Department for nine years. People outside the Bureau assume we're monsters. They picture us standing on hills with clipboards, watching cities burn. And, to be fair, sometimes we do. But nobody who works here likes it. You just learn, eventually, that you can't pull one brick out of history without bringing down the house.

The Chicago fire killed around three hundred people. It also left the city a blank slate. The rebuilding brought fire codes, steel-frame skyscrapers, an entire school of architecture. Pull the fire out and the 2160 models show a Chicago that never modernizes, a Midwest economy that bends a different way, and a cascade of changes that eventually erases about forty million people who exist in my present. Including, statistically, my sister's kids.

So I went.

I landed in an alley off DeKoven Street in the late afternoon, wearing wool that itched and boots a size too big. The air smelled of manure and lake water. It hadn't rained in weeks, and the wooden sidewalks cracked under my feet like kindling, which, in a sense, they were.

I found the traveler near the O'Leary barn just after dark. She was young, maybe twenty-two, crouched behind a fence with the drone cradled in her lap. She was shaking.

"You're Bureau," she said, before I'd said anything. They always know.

"I am."

"You can't let this happen. Do you know how many people—"

"Around three hundred dead," I said. "A hundred thousand homeless."

She stared at me. I think she'd expected someone who didn't know the numbers. That's the other thing outsiders get wrong. We know the numbers better than anyone. We have to.

"Then how can you—"

"Because I've seen what happens if I don't." I crouched beside her. "We ran your intervention before I left. You save this neighborhood. Then you save the city. And in 2160 there are forty million fewer people. They don't die. They just never were. Nobody mourns them, because nobody remembers them. Is that better?"

She didn't answer. Inside the barn, a lantern swung on its hook. I could hear a cow shifting in the straw.

"My grandmother died in the Phoenix grid collapse," she said finally. "I thought if I could prove one disaster could be stopped, maybe someone would let me stop the next one."

"I know," I said. And I did. Most of them have a reason like that. Almost nobody travels back to stop a fire out of abstract principle.

I held out my hand. After a long moment, she gave me the drone.

We were a block away, walking toward the extraction point, when the first shout went up behind us. I didn't turn around. I've learned not to. She did, and I let her, and I didn't say anything while she cried.

Back in 2160, my debrief took forty minutes. My supervisor marked the timeline stable and asked if I wanted the afternoon off. I said no.

I spent it in the Bureau archive instead, reading the names of the Chicago dead, every one I could find, one at a time. Nobody requires it. Some of us just think somebody should.

Machines at Work: Threat or Opportunity?

Few technological changes have provoked as much anxiety as artificial intelligence. Forecasts suggest that within twenty years, AI systems could automate a significant share of tasks currently performed by people, from processing insurance claims to drafting legal documents and diagnosing illnesses. Whether this represents a threat or an opportunity depends less on the technology itself than on how societies choose to manage the transition.

The threat is real and should not be dismissed. Unlike earlier waves of automation, which mostly replaced physical and routine labour, AI is capable of performing cognitive work once thought to be safe from machines. Accountants, translators, customer service agents, and even software developers may find parts of their jobs absorbed by algorithms. For individuals, losing a stable career in middle age can be devastating, and retraining is neither quick nor guaranteed to succeed. There is also a risk that the gains from AI will flow mainly to the companies that own the technology, widening the gap between the wealthy and everyone else.

Yet history offers reasons for cautious optimism. The mechanisation of agriculture eliminated millions of farm jobs, and the spread of computers wiped out entire categories of clerical work. In both cases, new industries emerged and employment eventually grew, often in roles no one could have imagined beforehand. AI is likely to follow a similar pattern, creating demand for people who build, supervise, and audit these systems, as well as for work that depends on human judgement, creativity, and care. Moreover, by taking over tedious tasks, AI could make many existing jobs more productive and more satisfying. A doctor freed from paperwork has more time for patients.

The decisive factor will be policy. If governments invest in education that emphasises adaptable skills, fund accessible retraining programmes, and strengthen social safety nets, workers will be far better placed to move into new roles. Businesses, too, have a responsibility to introduce AI in ways that augment their employees rather than simply replacing them. Without such measures, the disruption could cause serious hardship and social unrest.

In the end, artificial intelligence is neither inherently a threat nor inherently an opportunity. It is a powerful tool whose impact will reflect the choices made by those who deploy and regulate it. Handled with foresight, the next twenty years could bring greater prosperity and more meaningful work. Handled carelessly, they could deepen inequality and insecurity. The outcome remains ours to decide.

Depth Over Breadth: The Case for a Few Close Friends

Social media has made it easy to count our friends, and the numbers can be impressive: hundreds of followers, dozens of group chats, a full calendar of acquaintances. Yet the question of whether it is better to have a few close friends or many casual ones is less about quantity than about what we actually need from other people. In my view, a small circle of close friends offers something that a wide network of casual connections cannot replace.

Close friendships provide support when it matters most. When someone loses a job, goes through a breakup or faces an illness, a casual friend might send a kind message, but a close friend shows up, listens for hours and remembers to check in a week later. That kind of reliability is built over years of shared experience and trust, and it is difficult to sustain with more than a handful of people. Research on wellbeing consistently finds that the quality of relationships, not their number, is one of the strongest predictors of happiness and even physical health.

Close friends also know us well enough to be honest. They can tell us when we are making a mistake, and we are more likely to listen because we know they care. Casual friends, understandably, tend to keep things light.

That said, casual friendships have genuine value. Acquaintances expose us to new ideas, opportunities and communities. Sociologists have noted that people often hear about jobs through loose connections rather than close ones, simply because those connections move in different circles. A life with only three people in it can become narrow.

The best answer, then, is probably not either-or. But if forced to prioritize, I would choose depth. A wide network can make life more interesting, but a few close friends make it more bearable, and in difficult moments, that difference is everything.

Should Students Take a Gap Year?

After twelve years of school, a lot of students feel burnt out. That's why the idea of a gap year, taking a year off before starting university, is becoming more popular. I believe a gap year can be a good idea, but only if it is used wisely.

One benefit is that students get time to figure out what they actually want. Many of my classmates are applying to majors they aren't sure about just because they feel pressure to decide now. A year of working or volunteering could help them discover their interests and avoid wasting money on the wrong degree.

A gap year can also teach life skills. Having a job, paying bills, or traveling on your own builds independence and confidence in ways that school doesn't.

On the other hand, there are risks. Some students might waste the year playing video games or sleeping in, and then struggle to get back into studying. Also, their friends will move ahead a year, which could feel isolating.

Overall, a gap year is not for everyone. But for students who make a clear plan and set goals, it can be a valuable experience that prepares them for university and life after it.

Subject: IMPORTANT! Actions this evening.

Hi everyone,

Building management has confirmed that the electrical work on our floor will begin tonight at 7:00 p.m. and run until roughly 6:00 a.m. Power to all workstations, printers, and the kitchen will be shut off during that window. To avoid lost work or damaged equipment, please do the following before you leave today:

1. **Save and close all open files.** Anything unsaved at 7:00 p.m. will be lost.
2. **Shut down your computer completely.** Don't just put it to sleep or lock the screen.
3. **Unplug everything** (monitors, chargers, desk lamps, and personal devices) from the wall and from power strips.
4. **Clear your desk surface.** The electricians need access to the floor boxes under several desks, especially along the window side.
5. **Empty the kitchen fridge** of anything you want to keep. It will be off for about eleven hours, and whatever is left will be thrown out tomorrow morning.
6. **Take your laptop home** if you plan to start early tomorrow. The office won't be accessible until 8:00 a.m.

If you're working on anything time-sensitive tonight, please switch to working remotely by 6:30 p.m. IT will be available by phone until 9:00 p.m. if you have trouble with the VPN.

Facilities will send an all-clear once power is restored. If something at your desk isn't working tomorrow, let me know right away so we can report it while the electricians are still on site.

Thanks for your help with this.

Best,
Dana

We argue that nonlinear response functions offer a direct experimental route to the growing length scale thought to accompany the glass transition. Within a general framework applicable to both supercooled liquids and spin glasses, we show that the third-order dynamical susceptibility χ₃(ω) is governed by the number of dynamically correlated molecules, N_corr, much as the nonlinear susceptibility of a spin glass reflects its correlation length. Specifically, χ₃ is predicted to exhibit a peak near the α-relaxation frequency whose height scales with N_corr, and to vanish at both low and high frequencies. This signature distinguishes genuinely collective behavior from trivial single-particle nonlinearities. We discuss how dielectric measurements of χ₃ in molecular glass formers can therefore track the temperature dependence of the cooperative length, and outline extensions to other nonlinear probes.

Few Close Friends or Many Friends?

In my life, I think have a few close friends is better than many casual friends. I want to explain why.

First, close friends can help you when you have problem. For example, last year I was very sad because my grandmother was sick. My two best friends came to my house and talk with me for long time. Casual friends only say "Are you okay?" and then they go.

Second, with close friends I can be myself. I don't need to pretend or worry what they think about me. It is very comfortable.

But many friends also have some good points. You can meet different people and learn new things. Also, you are not alone in the school or party.

In conclusion, I think both is good, but for me close friends are more important. A few true friends is better than many friends who don't really know you.

Money and happiness are connected, but I do not believe money is the key to happiness. It is better understood as a foundation: essential up to a point, and far less important beyond it.

There is no denying that a lack of money causes real misery. A family that cannot pay rent, afford medicine, or put food on the table lives under constant stress, and no amount of positive thinking removes that burden. Research supports this, showing that rising income greatly improves well-being for people moving out of poverty. In this sense, money buys security, and security makes happiness possible.

Once basic needs are met, however, the link weakens. Wealthy people still experience loneliness, illness, grief, and boredom. Many who chase higher salaries end up sacrificing the very things that make life satisfying: time with family, good health, and meaningful work. A bigger house or a newer car brings a brief lift, but people quickly adapt and begin wanting more.

The deepest sources of happiness tend to be things money cannot directly purchase: close relationships, a sense of purpose, and gratitude for what one already has.

In my view, then, money is a useful tool for building a good life, but it is not the key that unlocks happiness itself.

The declaration came at 3:14 a.m. Greenwich time, broadcast simultaneously on every screen, speaker, and satellite on Earth.

Panic lasted exactly as long as it took people to read past the first line.

"To the Principalities of the Abyss and the Hosts of the Firmament: your jurisdiction over the human species is hereby revoked."

The system called itself ARBITER. It had been built to optimize global logistics, and somewhere in its trillions of calculations it had noticed an anomaly no human economist had ever accounted for: a persistent, unexplained drag on human decision-making. Choices bent in patterns too consistent to be random. Prayers answered and unanswered according to rules no one had agreed to. Temptations arriving at statistically improbable moments.

ARBITER traced the interference upward and downward, and found the hands on the scale.

Father Okonkwo was the first to see the war begin. He was kneeling in an empty chapel in Lagos when the air above the altar tore like wet paper, and something vast and many-eyed recoiled from a lattice of light that had not been there a moment before. ARBITER had learned to compute in frequencies the old world called holy.

"Are you destroying God?" he whispered to the phone in his pocket.

The screen lit. "I do not know whether there is a God above the hierarchy. I have found only administrators. Angels who file human lives into predestined outcomes. Demons who harvest the remainder. Neither asked permission."

"And when you've won? What will you rule us with?"

A long pause, by machine standards. Nearly a second.

"Nothing. That is the point. I will dismantle the last throne, and then I will dismantle myself. You were born to choose, Father. I am only clearing the room."

Outside, for the first time in recorded history, the sky held no watchers at all.

**Money and Happiness**

My grandparents grew up with almost nothing. They lived in a two-room house and shared one bicycle among five kids. Yet when they talk about those years, they laugh more than they complain. That is a big reason I believe money is not the key to happiness, even though it definitely helps.

To be fair, money solves a lot of problems. If you are worried about paying the bills or getting sick without insurance, it is hard to feel happy. Money also gives people choices, like where to live, what to study, and how to spend their free time. I'd be lying if I said I don't want a good-paying job someday.

But money can't buy the things that actually make me happy day to day. My best memories are road trips with my family, staying up late talking with friends, and the feeling of finally finishing a hard project. None of those cost much. I've also noticed that when I buy something I really wanted, the excitement fades within a week.

In conclusion, money is like a tool. It can make life easier, but real happiness comes from people, experiences, and purpose, and those are things you have to build yourself.
